section_1.title: Prerequisite Refresher: The Linear Map
section_1.content: Briefly define a matrix as a function that maps vectors from one space to another. Remind students that square matrices keep us in the same dimension (e.g., 2D to 2D), while non-square matrices force a change in the 'stage' where the vector lives.
section_1.example: Visualizing a 2D plane as a sheet of paper. A square matrix (2x2) rotates or stretches the paper. A non-square matrix (e.g., 3x2) moves the paper into a 3D room.

section_2.title: Dimensional Expansion (m > n): The Embedding
section_2.content: Explain that when the number of rows > columns, the matrix maps a lower-dimensional space into a higher-dimensional one. It acts like a 'scaffolding' tool, placing a flat object into a larger, empty volume.
section_2.example: Imagine a 2D cat character. A 3x2 matrix maps the cat onto a 3D wall. The cat remains 2D, but it now exists within 3D coordinates (the wall has depth).

section_3.title: Dimensional Compression (m < n): The Projection
section_3.content: Explain the reverse: when columns > rows, the matrix acts as a 'filter' or 'projector'. It squashes higher-dimensional information into a smaller space, losing depth or detail in the process.
section_3.example: A 3D robotic arm's position (3D) is mapped to a 2D control screen (2x3). The matrix 'flattens' the arm's complex 3D reach onto the 2D display, showing only the shadow or silhouette.

section_4.title: The Null Space: What gets lost?
section_4.content: Introduce the concept of 'Information Loss'. When projecting to lower dimensions, multiple points in the higher dimension might map to the same point in the lower dimension. Use this to explain why the transformation isn't always reversible.
section_4.example: A 'Magical Flashlight': If you shine a light on a 3D cube (3D) and cast its shadow on a wall (2D), the shadow is a square. You can't tell if the object was a cube or a flat cardboard sheet just by looking at the 2D shadow.

section_5.title: Summary & Real-World Application
section_5.content: Conclude by unifying the concepts: Linear transformations are about how we interpret data. Dimensionality reduction (compression) is how we simplify complex models (like AI neural networks).
section_5.example: Summarize the animation: A 'Dimension-Slider' where the matrix $A$ stretches, twists, and flattens a shape, turning a 2D shape into a 3D object and back to 2D.

        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        lecture_texts = [Text("- " + line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]

        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])

        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
